answer: Reputation-decayed entry pricing. Each new identity starts on an oasis of zero history; its registration price rises with the density of identities sharing its network knoll (IP range, funding source, timing cluster). To anchor a new identity, an attacker must either pay the surging price for that crowded knoll or spend weeks building sparse, unrelated history. Cost scales superlinearly with cluster size, so a thousand-identity farm pays thousands of times the marginal single-identity price.
